old: Group 15 forms 3− ions, so phosphorus forms P3−, named phosphide.
new: Phosphorus is in group 15, so it has 5 valence electrons. Gaining 3 more gives it a full octet, like argon, so it forms P3−. A simple anion keeps the element’s root and ends in -ide: phosphide.

old: CHCl3: dispersion and dipole–dipole (no H on N, O, or F).
new: Every molecule has dispersion forces. CHCl3 is also polar: the three C–Cl bonds are polar and the tetrahedral shape does not cancel them, so it has dipole–dipole forces too. Its only H is on carbon, not on N, O, or F, so there is no hydrogen bonding: dispersion and dipole–dipole.
why: explanation: explain why it is polar and why no H-bonding

old: NH3 gains H+ to form NH4+: a Brønsted–Lowry base (proton acceptor).
new: The Arrhenius definition needs a base to release OH−, and NH3 has none. The Brønsted–Lowry definition only asks that a base accept a proton: the lone pair on N takes an H+ to form NH4+. So NH3 is a Brønsted–Lowry base (proton acceptor).
